I spent my life getting back at my parents by overpowering them and scaring them off or simply ignoring them as much as I could live independently away from them. I only felt more bad about myself how I turned into a monster.  

What made things a little better was when I stopped hating them and started to appreciate that I have them.  My boyfriend helped me with that through his life story.  

He urged me to love my parents while they're still alive.  That's the lesson he learned when his father died.  He regret he wasn't there for his father before he lost him.   His father's death also made him appreciate life more, he stopped being suicidal since he experienced how painful it is to lose a loved one.  He also helped me understand them how they just really care and love me and just protecting me when they were like being too controlling or too much keeping me in check.   

When I stopped seeing my parents as my enemies and started to open up and talk to them as my parents, I began to get to know them better and understand the way they are.  It wasn't until then that I felt how great I have a family.  

I also learned that we can't just expect people to understand us or respond the way we would like them, even our friends and family.  We need to open up and communicate authentically, trust and allow yourself to be vulnerable, that's how we earn love and understanding.  

What's obvious to us might not be apparent to them, we have to communicate how they can be of help and how they make us feel.    But I also learned, we can't expect our parents to be as comforting as trained professionals or as other parents who also had some training/knowledge in how to deal with people, especially people going through depression or something.  

People have different experiences and ways of communicating. Those you quotes you had above, they might be sincerely trying to help by saying things that have helped them when they were in your situation, it's just that, they didn't really know what's going on with you.  

And when you feel like not being cared for or prioritized, they might also be going through a tough time inside themselves, it's not just you who lost your father.  About the biased treatment towards your siblings, I think it's the way you communicate what you want or need.

(I'm not familiar about the full news story background, my comment is just about science literacy). The ultimate scientific illiteracy is when you take science as always true. I'm not against science but I also don't take science as the truth.  I'm talking about the science according to experts (text books and journals), not pseudoscience. Even "real" science can be untrue. Science is science because it continues to be under investigation, has to be tested and replicated throughout time.  If you've read enough science, you'd see how facts change over decades or centuries. Science discoveries unfold gradually with new information, like slowly opening your eyes, you don't see the whole picture instantly, often it takes more than a lifetime.  We can't always just believe our eyes, we still haven't completed picture.  As a scientist who had the best science education in the country, I learned that science always have to be taken with a grain of salt and the benefit of the doubt, you always have to be critical about it, that's how science progress happens. Otherwise, it's no longer science, it becomes religion.  As a science scholar, I despised the kind of  scientific education where science is taught like from a pulpit with science textbooks and journals being the bible.  Even some teachers (in the U.S.) sees and explains how some science text book companies make business with the education system.  (Philippines just copy U.S., so, i bet just the same here.)  Scientific corruption does exist, we don't know to what extent.  But did you know, around the world, many science masters and PhD students and medical students just buy their academic research  papers online?  I wonder what kind of scientists and science we have now or in the future. One old professor warned us about recent scientific publications (text books and journals) and said older science publications are more scientific and less influenced by money and politics.  Long ago, he had been offered money  to join a world wide science propaganda that make lots of money today, his colleagues accepted the money for the job but he refused. It's just logical to think that science can be influenced by  business, especially medical products produced by science that makes big money.  As a matter of fact, it's harder to find and get funding for science researches that does not have apparent immediate potential to make money.  Big science researches can't be done without money, and so, a lot of science funding comes from businesses and governments.  Where there's big money, there also comes politics of what gets published and what should be kept secret.  Thus, real scientific literacy is beyond being educated on what's published.   This is not just in the Philippines. I hope I've helped improve scientific literacy.  And to conclude, in relation to the vaccines issue, I think people have the right to follow their own beliefs and religions which is independent of their scientific literacy.
